key_terms.meaning: One shared set of wires on which many nodes exchange many signals using addressed messages instead of separate wires per signal.
Any device connected to the bus; a node may be an ECU, a sensor module or the diagnostic connector.
A small computer with a microcontroller, memory, I/O drivers and a bus interface that controls one subsystem of the vehicle.
A node with two or more bus interfaces that forwards selected messages between buses and blocks the rest.
The bundle of wires, connectors and clamps in the vehicle; its mass and cost fall sharply when a bus replaces point-to-point wiring.
The maximum data rate a channel can carry, measured in bits per second (bit/s); CAN gives up to 1 Mbit/s, CAN FD up to 8 Mbit/s in the data phase.
The time from a node deciding to send a message to the message being available at the receiver, in milliseconds or microseconds.
The property that the worst-case time for a message to reach its receiver can be calculated in advance and is guaranteed.
CAN logic levels: dominant = 0 (bus driven low, wins) and recessive = 1 (bus released); if any node sends 0 the bus reads 0.
Bit-by-bit competition at the start of a CAN frame in which a node sending recessive 1 while the bus is dominant 0 stops transmitting and retries later.
CAN with Flexible Data-rate: same arbitration as CAN, but a faster data phase (up to 8 Mbit/s) and a payload up to 64 bytes.
Local Interconnect Network: a single-wire, master-slave bus at up to 20 kbit/s used for cheap body functions such as window and mirror switches.
A dual-channel, time-triggered bus at up to 10 Mbit/s per channel in which each node transmits only in its assigned time slot, giving fixed latency.
A switched 100 Mbit/s or 1 Gbit/s network using 100BASE-T1/1000BASE-T1 single twisted pair, used as the backbone between domains.
A five-character code such as P0301 that names a fault; the first letter gives the system (P powertrain, B body, C chassis, U network).
The dashboard 'check engine' lamp that OBD-II requires the ECU to switch on when an emissions-related fault is confirmed.
A set of coding rules that bans unsafe or ambiguous C constructs so that static analysis can prove the code avoids undefined behaviour.
Automotive Safety Integrity Level, A to D (D strictest), assigned from the severity, exposure and controllability of a hazard; it sets the rigour the safety lifecycle must show.
Vehicle-to-Everything: message exchange between a vehicle and other vehicles (V2V), roadside units (V2I), pedestrians (V2P) and the network (V2N).
A fixed roadside radio and computer that broadcasts traffic, signal-phase and hazard data to passing vehicles.
Vehicular Ad hoc Network: vehicles that form a network among themselves with no fixed infrastructure, using each other as relays.
Forwarding a packet to the neighbour that lies closest to the destination's known coordinates instead of keeping a route table.
Dedicated Short-Range Communications: short-range radio for road safety, allocated around 5.9 GHz with channels of 10 MHz.
Wireless Access in Vehicular Environments: the IEEE 1609 family of standards that sits above IEEE 802.11p and handles multi-channel timing, networking and security.

takeaways: A shared bus cuts harness mass, cost and connector count, but it makes bandwidth, latency and determinism design problems that point-to-point wiring did not have.
CAN resolves collisions during arbitration instead of after them: the lowest numerical identifier wins and no message is destroyed.
CAN FD keeps CAN's arbitration and frame structure but shortens the data phase and allows up to 64 bytes, which suits software updates and sensor fusion.
LIN, FlexRay and automotive Ethernet are not competitors; they sit at different cost, speed and determinism points and are joined by a gateway.
OBD-II is a legal standard, not a manufacturer feature: one connector, one set of messages and one code format for emissions-related faults.
MISRA C reduces coding faults and ISO 26262 manages the remaining risk; the two together form the evidence a safety case needs.
V2X extends perception beyond line of sight, which matters at blind corners and in mixed traffic where cameras and radar see too late.
DSRC, IEEE 802.11p and WAVE are three layers of one system: radio, MAC/PHY, and the networking, timing and security stack above them.
bank_note: Long answers here mix a definition, a frame-level or layer-level diagram, and an Indian-context justification, so always draw the bus topology or protocol stack and then argue cost, latency or safety.

bank.q: Explain why modern vehicles use data buses instead of point-to-point wiring. Cover harness mass, cost, diagnostics and the terms bandwidth, latency and determinism.
outline: Point-to-point wiring grows as the square of the number of signals
Bus: one two-wire medium, many nodes, addressed messages
Harness mass and cost saving, easier fault-finding
Bandwidth in bit/s and what limits it
Latency and why safety functions need bounded latency
Determinism: worst-case time calculable in advance
Gateway needed to join buses of different speeds

bank.q: Describe the CAN data frame field by field and explain how bit-wise arbitration works using dominant and recessive levels.
outline: Frame: SOF, identifier, RTR, control, data (0-8 bytes), CRC, ACK, EOF, IFS
Dominant = 0, recessive = 1; wired-AND behaviour
Node sending recessive sees dominant and backs off
Lower numerical identifier wins
Loser retries, no data lost, no time lost
CRC and ACK fields, error frames, fault confinement

bank.q: Compare LIN, FlexRay and automotive Ethernet on topology, data rate, determinism and typical use.
outline: LIN: single wire, master-slave, up to 20 kbit/s, schedule table, body switches
FlexRay: dual channel, up to 10 Mbit/s per channel, TDMA static slots plus dynamic segment, x-by-wire
Ethernet: switched star, 100 Mbit/s or 1 Gbit/s, not deterministic by default, backbone and camera links
Cost and node count comparison
Role of gateway between them

bank.q: Explain the OBD-II standard: connector, pin assignment, communication, PIDs, DTC format and the malfunction indicator lamp.
outline: 16-pin J1962 connector under the dash within reach of the driver
Pins 4 and 5 ground, pin 16 battery positive, pins 6 and 14 CAN
Five protocols allowed, CAN mandatory on later vehicles
Mode services such as live data and stored codes
PID request/response for emissions data
DTC: letter, four digits, P/B/C/U system groups
MIL on after confirmed emissions fault, freeze frame stored

bank.q: Explain how ISO 26262 assigns an ASIL and what the safety lifecycle demands at that level.
outline: Item definition, hazard analysis and risk assessment
Severity, exposure, controllability classes
ASIL A to D and QM, from the risk table
Safety goals, functional safety concept, technical safety concept
Safety lifecycle phases and work products as evidence
Hardware metrics and software techniques scale with ASIL
Confirmation measures and independent assessment

bank.q: Three nodes start sending CAN frames with identifiers 0x123, 0x0F1 and 0x2A0 at the same instant. Trace the arbitration bit by bit, name the winner, and state when the losers retransmit.
outline: Write identifiers in binary, MSB first after SOF
Compare bit by bit; first difference decides
Node sending recessive 1 while bus is dominant 0 becomes receiver
0x0F1 wins because its identifier is numerically smallest
Losers set a pending flag and retry after the interframe space
No data corrupted, only delay for the losers
Note that identifier value doubles as message priority

bank.q: A powertrain CAN bus at 500 kbit/s carries twelve messages. Explain how you would calculate bus load and worst-case latency for one message, and what you would do if the load crosses 70 percent.
outline: Frame time = number of bits including stuffing divided by bit rate
Bus load = sum of frame times per period divided by period
Worst-case latency = blocking by lower-priority frame + own transmission + queueing
Effect of stuff bits and of error frames
Options: raise bit rate, split onto a second bus, move to CAN FD, lengthen periods
Keep margin for future messages

bank.q: Prepare a bus allocation plan for a car with body, powertrain, chassis and infotainment domains. Choose the bus for each link and justify each choice with numbers.
outline: Body: LIN for switches and motors, up to 20 kbit/s
Powertrain and chassis: CAN or CAN FD, 500 kbit/s to 2 Mbit/s
Steering and braking by-wire: FlexRay time slots for fixed latency
Camera, radar and infotainment: automotive Ethernet 100 Mbit/s or 1 Gbit/s
Central gateway between all domains, message filtering
Diagnostic access through OBD-II port on CAN
Cost per node and wiring mass as deciding factors

bank.q: A scan tool reads DTC P0301 with a freeze frame showing 2,400 rpm, 62 km/h and 35 percent load. Explain how the code is interpreted, what P0301 means, and the steps you would take next.
outline: P = powertrain, 0 = generic SAE code, 3 = ignition system, 01 = cylinder 1 misfire
Freeze frame stores conditions at the moment of the fault
Misfire detected from crankshaft speed fluctuation
Check ignition, injector, compression, wiring to coil
MIL behaviour and drive-cycle clearing of the code
Use live data and mode 6 results to confirm repair

bank.q: Analyse the IEEE 1609 WAVE stack: what each of 1609.1, 1609.2, 1609.3 and 1609.4 does, and how the stack sits on IEEE 802.11p and DSRC channels.
outline: DSRC: 5.9 GHz band, 10 MHz channels, one control channel and service channels
802.11p: OFDM PHY and MAC derived from 802.11a, outside BSS context
1609.1: resource manager for remote applications
1609.2: security, certificates and signed messages
1609.3: WSMP networking and WAVE service advertisements
1609.4: multi-channel operation, synchronised control and service intervals
Why low latency matters and why IPv6 alone is not always used

bank.q: Analyse the characteristics and challenges of a VANET: mobility, road-constrained topology, intermittent links, and why position-based routing suits it better than table-driven routing.
outline: Nodes move at high speed, topology changes every few seconds
Movement constrained by roads, so position predicts the future
No fixed infrastructure, power and storage not limited
Link breaks cause route repair storms in AODV-style protocols
Greedy perimeter stateless routing: greedy forwarding then perimeter recovery
Localisation accuracy and GPS loss, security and privacy issues
Broadcast storm problem in dense traffic

bank.q: Evaluate whether DSRC or cellular V2X is the better choice for intersection warning and platooning in Indian mixed traffic, giving technical and deployment reasons.
outline: DSRC: direct link, low latency, works without cellular coverage, needs roadside units
Cellular V2X: wider coverage, uses existing towers, sidelink mode for direct links
Latency and reliability comparison at intersections
Mixed traffic with two-wheelers and pedestrians needs V2P
Cost of roadside units and spectrum availability
Security and certificate management in both
Likely answer: hybrid, with direct links for safety and cellular for cloud services

bank.q: A steer-by-wire system must be certified to ASIL D and runs on FlexRay. Evaluate the combined role of MISRA C coding rules and the ISO 26262 safety lifecycle as evidence.
outline: Hazard analysis gives high severity, exposure and controllability, hence ASIL D
Safety goal and technical safety concept for steering
MISRA C rules remove undefined behaviour and aid static analysis
Coding standard required as a work product, with tool qualification
FlexRay static slots give bounded latency, supporting the timing argument
Evidence: traceability, verification reports, safety case
Limits: MISRA C alone is not safety, ISO 26262 alone is not code quality

bank.q: Evaluate the claim that connected-vehicle electronics can soon be merged with the infotainment unit, using V2X latency, security and safety arguments.
outline: Infotainment has long update cycles and large software stacks
V2X needs bounded latency and a certified path
Safety criticality of warning messages, ASIL considerations
Attack surface widens if one unit handles both
Virtualisation and domain controllers as a middle path
Shared antenna and radio savings as the benefit
Verdict: keep safety-critical V2X on a separate partition with its own certification

glossary.def: A single shared communication medium on which several nodes exchange addressed messages.
A device attached to the bus that can send and receive messages.
A node that joins two or more buses and forwards only the messages that need to cross.
The complete set of wires and connectors in the vehicle.
A guarantee that the worst-case message delay is known before the system is built.
The CAN logic 0, produced by actively pulling the bus to a low differential voltage; it overrides a recessive bit.
The CAN logic 1, produced by releasing the bus so that the terminators hold it at the idle level.
The bit-wise contest at the start of a CAN frame that lets the lowest identifier transmit without collision.
CAN with a faster data phase and payloads of up to 64 bytes, sharing CAN's arbitration.
A cheap single-wire master-slave bus for body electronics, up to 20 kbit/s.
A dual-channel time-triggered bus for safety-critical chassis functions, up to 10 Mbit/s per channel.
A switched single-pair Ethernet network used as the high-bandwidth backbone of a vehicle.
A legal diagnostic standard fixing the 16-pin connector, message set and code format for emissions faults.
In the bus context, the layer that frames bits, checks errors and controls access to the medium.
A short header carrying identifier and data-length information used by CAN and similar buses.
A rule set restricting C so that risky constructs and undefined behaviour are removed from embedded code.
Automotive Safety Integrity Level, from A to D, giving the rigour required by a safety goal.
The documented argument and evidence that a system meets its safety goals.
Diagnostic trouble code, a five-character identifier of a specific fault.
Vehicle-to-Everything communication covering vehicle, infrastructure, pedestrian and network peers.
Roadside unit, fixed infrastructure that talks to passing vehicles.
An ad hoc network formed by moving vehicles without fixed infrastructure.
Dedicated Short-Range Communications, the 5.9 GHz radio service for road safety.
The IEEE 1609 stack above IEEE 802.11p handling multi-channel use, networking and security.
WAVE Short Message Protocol, a lightweight network protocol for safety messages defined in IEEE 1609.3.
